metadata.title: National contexts and information and communication technology in education: A systematic review of PISA studies

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a systematic review that synthesizes findings from previously published PISA-based studies rather than re-analyzing PISA microdata. Therefore, no student-level sampling weights, replicate weights, or PV-handling procedures are applied by the authors in this paper. The included primary studies may have used PISA’s complex survey design and PV-based scaling for cognitive outcomes, but those technical choices are not re-implemented here. For interpretation, the review’s conclusions reflect the direction and reported significance of relationships across studies, not pooled, weight-adjusted effect estimates from a single harmonized PISA dataset.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because this paper does not conduct an empirical analysis of PISA student microdata; it synthesizes results from 29 included PISA-based studies. Missing-data handling is not reported because the review does not perform dataset-level imputation or deletion procedures; instead, it applies inclusion/exclusion criteria to studies and extracts reported findings. As a result, there is no single analytic dataset for which missingness would be imputed or handled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper conducts a systematic review using Web of Science (SSCI and ESCI) with PRISMA screening. Inclusion criteria required peer-reviewed, English-language studies using PISA data and analyzing both student- and country-level variables in the same statistical model (via multilevel modeling or explicit country indicators in single-level models). Studies that analyzed countries separately without including country-level factors were excluded; only full-text articles were retained. The final inclusion comprised 29 studies; the review also reports that 31 responses were coded across 15 countries based on first-author affiliations, but these are not PISA respondent countries and are not treated as an analytic student sample.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This article is a systematic review of PISA-based studies examining how student- and country-level ICT factors relate to learning outcomes, and how national contexts moderate these relationships. It does not re-analyze PISA microdata; instead, it screens and codes 29 peer-reviewed English-language studies from Web of Science using PRISMA procedures. Across the included studies, the review reports that most evidence concerns cognitive outcomes (reading, mathematics, science), with fewer studies addressing affective and behavioral outcomes. The review synthesizes patterns such as generally positive associations for ICT attitudes (e.g., self-confidence, competence, interest, autonomy) and more mixed or often negative associations for ICT access/use depending on context (home vs school; classroom lessons vs outside lessons). It also summarizes country-level variance using reported ICC ranges and describes moderation types (facilitating, diminishing, buffering, exacerbating, minimal). Because no pooled ML model or PV-based scaling is estimated in this paper, the findings are descriptive of the literature rather than effect-size estimates from a unified dataset. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is intentionally sparse in fields that would normally be populated for an empirical ML/PISA re-analysis (e.g., total_students, countries with n_students, PV handling, missing-data strategy, and ML techniques). The paper is a systematic review that synthesizes previously published PISA-based quantitative studies rather than training or evaluating ML models on PISA microdata. Consequently, there is no single assessment cycle/grade/domain dataset used by the authors for model estimation, and no student-level weighting or PV computation performed within this manuscript.
